keep: The Greeley letter is read as indifference to slavery. He wrote it a month after reading his cabinet the proclamation that would free people.
lede: He wrote that if he could save the Union without freeing any slave, he would. The draft that freed them was already in his hand.
copy: By the summer of 1862 Abraham Lincoln was being pressed by abolitionists and radical Republicans to free the slaves. On 17 July Congress passed the Second Confiscation Act, giving Union forces the right to free slaves held by rebels. He had already drafted what he called a preliminary proclamation. He read it first to William Seward and Gideon Welles on 13 July. Seward, by the Library of Congress's account, said it would be viewed as the last measure of an exhausted government. On 22 July Lincoln read it to the whole cabinet. Stanton wanted it out at once; Montgomery Blair foresaw defeat in the autumn elections. Lincoln kept it, and waited for a victory.

A month later Horace Greeley's Tribune printed 'The Prayer of Twenty Millions', accusing him of reluctance to use the powers Congress had given him. Lincoln answered on 22 August, in a rival paper. 'My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union, and is not either to save or to destroy slavery. If I could save the Union without freeing any slave I would do it.' It is the most quoted proof that he did not care. He wrote it with the draft already written. The letter ends: 'I intend no modification of my oft-expressed personal wish that all men everywhere could be free.' The preliminary proclamation followed on 22 September, four days after the Union victory at Antietam.

The final text of 1 January 1863 freed people only where the states were in rebellion. It named the exceptions: thirteen Louisiana parishes, New Orleans among them, the forty-eight counties of West Virginia, and seven more in Virginia, including Norfolk and Portsmouth, all 'left precisely as if this proclamation were not issued'. The loyal border states it did not touch. Its promise depended on Union armies, and it opened those armies to Black men; by the end of the war almost 200,000 had served. The Thirteenth Amendment passed the Senate in April 1864 and the House on 31 January 1865, by 119 votes to 56. It was ratified on 6 December 1865, after his death.

bio.why: A two-time Pulitzer winner's single-volume life, following Lincoln's own knowledge at each moment, capturing his growth and his limits. For the cabinet, pair it with Doris Kearns Goodwin's Team of Rivals (2005). This house has read the documents, not Donald.

contested: What the Greeley letter was for. One reading takes it at its word: Union first, slavery a means. Another, the one this entry leans on, reads it as cover, written by a man who had already decided and was preparing the North for it; the Library of Congress's account, that his mind was made up as to the substance by July, supports that. The sharpest case against both is Lerone Bennett Jr.'s Forced into Glory (2000), which argues that Lincoln was pushed into emancipation and never wanted it. Eric Foner's The Fiery Trial (2010) is the standard answer, that his views on slavery moved under pressure and that the movement is the story. This house has read neither book and states both only as leads. The documents settle the order of events. They do not settle what was in his head.
